entities.name: National Museum of Anthropology
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Museum of Anthropology (Museo Nacional de Antropología) in Mexico City, opened in 1964 in Pedro Ramírez Vázquez's architectural masterpiece in Chapultepec Park, is the Western Hemisphere's greatest pre-Columbian museum — holding the world's most comprehensive collection of Mesoamerican artifacts, including the Aztec Sun Stone (incorrectly called the Aztec Calendar), the Jade Mask of Pakal, and over 600,000 archaeological objects spanning 11,000 years of Mexican civilization. The museum's political purpose — celebrating Mexico's indigenous heritage as the foundation of national identity — was as deliberate as its architectural magnificence.

President López Mateos commissioned the museum as a statement of national identity: Mexico is not a European colonial extension but an indigenous civilization that absorbed and transformed Spanish conquest. Pedro Ramírez Vázquez's building, centered on a massive umbrella-canopy fountain sustained by a single pillar (the 'Umbrella of Tláloc'), creates a ceremonial sequence from Mesoamerican outdoor plazas to interior galleries. The first room presents early Mexican hominid fossils to assert pre-European American habitation.

The Aztec Sun Stone (1427 CE), weighing 24 tons and discovered beneath Mexico City's main plaza in 1790, is the museum's central artifact — a solar calendar and ritual object that has become the symbol of Mexican national identity. The Jade Mask of Pakal (683 CE), from Palenque's royal tomb, represents Maya artistic achievement. The museum's 12 permanent rooms present 11,000 years of civilization — from Paleolithic hunters to Aztec empire — arguing for Mexico's indigenous roots as the true foundation of national character.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology — deliberately designed to argue that Mexican national identity is rooted in indigenous Mesoamerican civilization rather than Spanish colonialism — became the most politically consequential museum building in the Western Hemisphere.
